name: NTP, SNMP and Syslog
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Configure NTP, decode syslog severities and destinations, and explain SNMP polling, traps and version security.

lesson.intro: When something breaks at 2 a.m., three quiet protocols decide whether you can work out what happened. NTP keeps every device's clock in agreement, syslog records what each device saw, and SNMP lets a management station watch the whole network and raise alerts. The CCNA expects you to configure NTP, know syslog facilities and all eight severity levels, and explain how SNMP works and how its versions differ in security.
objectives: Configure NTP client/server and server mode, and explain stratum and reference clocks
Read show ntp status and show ntp associations, and design NTP with redundant servers, a fallback clock and loopbacks
Decode a syslog message and list the eight severity levels in order with their numbers
Send log messages to the console, vty sessions, the buffer and a syslog server at the right level
Explain SNMP managers, agents, MIBs, OIDs and messages, and compare the security of versions 1, 2c and 3

sections.title: Why time matters
sections.body:
Two routers log the same outage. R1 says the link dropped at 09:14:07. R2 says 17:52:40 the previous day, because nobody ever set its clock. Now try to rebuild the story of an outage across 40 devices, a firewall and a few servers. Synchronized clocks are what turn a pile of logs into a timeline.

Accurate time matters for more than logs:

- **Troubleshooting and investigations**: matching events across devices, and with server and firewall logs, during an outage or a security incident.
- **Certificates and security**: certificates have validity dates. A device whose clock is far off may reject a perfectly good certificate as not yet valid, or accept an expired one. Authentication systems and audit records also rely on correct time.
- **Time-based features**: time-based ACLs and scheduled jobs only work if the clock is right.

A Cisco device keeps a software clock. After a reload it starts from a hardware calendar (on platforms that have one) or from a default date, often years in the past. You can set it by hand: `clock timezone` and `clock summer-time` in global configuration mode, then `clock set` in privileged EXEC mode. `show clock` displays it. A leading asterisk, as in `*09:14:07.123 UTC Mon Mar 1 1993`, means the time is not authoritative: nothing has synchronized it.

Setting clocks by hand does not scale, and clocks drift. **NTP (Network Time Protocol)** keeps them synchronized automatically. Devices exchange timestamps over **UDP port 123** and keep making small adjustments, so devices on a LAN typically agree to within milliseconds.

A good habit from the official guide: set the time zone and a roughly correct time first, then enable NTP. The device starts close to the right time and synchronizes faster.
sections.code:
R1(config)# clock timezone EST -5
R1(config)# clock summer-time EDT recurring
R1(config)# end
R1# clock set 20:52:49 21 October 2025
R1# show clock
20:52:55.051 EDT Tue Oct 21 2025
sections.tip: NTP uses UDP 123. Set the time zone before you set the time, because clock set is read in the configured zone.
sections.pitfall: Ignoring the asterisk in show clock or in log timestamps. It means the clock has never been synchronized, so those timestamps cannot be trusted.

check.question: Why can a router with a badly wrong clock fail to set up certificate-based connections such as HTTPS?
choices: Certificates have validity dates, so a wrong clock can make a valid certificate look expired or not yet valid
Certificates are encrypted with the current time as the key
NTP and certificates share UDP port 123
The router's clock sets the TCP sequence numbers
check.explanation: Certificate checks compare the validity period with the local clock. If the clock is years off, valid certificates fail the check. Time is not used as an encryption key, and NTP's port has nothing to do with certificates.

sections.title: NTP modes and stratum
sections.body:
Cisco devices use two main NTP commands, and the exam wants you to know exactly what each one makes the device do.

- `ntp server 10.0.0.1` puts the device in **client/server mode**. It acts as an NTP client and synchronizes its clock to 10.0.0.1. Once synchronized, it is also willing to serve time to any device that points at it. Most routers and switches run this way.
- `ntp master [stratum]` puts the device in **server mode**: it serves time from its own internal clock and synchronizes to nobody. The stratum defaults to **8** and can be set from 1 to 15.

A third mode is less common: `ntp peer 10.0.0.2` (symmetric active mode) makes two devices exchange time with each other, so either can synchronize to the other. Two core routers that follow the same outside servers sometimes peer as a backup.

**Stratum** measures distance from an authoritative time source. A **reference clock**, such as a GPS receiver or an atomic clock, is the source of truth, and a server attached directly to one is **stratum 1**. A device that synchronizes to a stratum 1 server becomes stratum 2, its clients stratum 3, and so on: **each client adds 1 to its server's stratum**. Lower is better, and a device that can reach several servers prefers the lowest stratum. NTP treats 15 as the highest usable value; a device that would end up at 16 considers the time unusable, which is why an unsynchronized clock shows stratum 16.

The example builds the chain used in the official guide. R3 runs `ntp master 2`, so it serves time at stratum 2. R2 is a client of R3, so it becomes stratum 3, and it is also the server for R1. R1 is a client of R2 and ends up at stratum 4.

The NTP standards use two more names you may meet: a **primary server** takes its time from a reference clock and runs at stratum 1, and a **secondary server** is one in client/server mode, getting its time from another NTP server.
sections.code:
R1 ------------ R2 ------------ R3
client/server   client/server   server only
stratum 4       stratum 3       stratum 2

! R3: server mode, from its own clock, at stratum 2
R3(config)# ntp master 2
! R2: client of R3, then a server for R1
R2(config)# ntp server 172.16.3.3
! R1: client of R2
R1(config)# ntp server 172.16.2.2
sections.tip: ntp server means "I am a client of that address." ntp master means "I am the clock."
sections.pitfall: Reading ntp server as 'make this router a server'. It makes the router a client of that server. Server-only mode is ntp master.

activity.title: Lab: sync the clock with NTP
activity.prompt: R2 must take its time from the NTP server at 10.0.0.1. Configure it, then run show ntp associations and show ntp status. On real gear the * and the synchronized status take a few minutes to appear, so focus on what each field means.

check.question: R1's only NTP command is `ntp server 10.1.1.1`. How does R1 behave?
choices: As an NTP server only, using its internal clock
As an NTP client only, never serving time to others
As a client of 10.1.1.1, and a server for others once synchronized
As an NTP server only after it is reloaded
check.explanation: ntp server puts the device in client/server mode: it synchronizes to 10.1.1.1 and, once synchronized, can serve time to other devices. Server-only mode from the internal clock is ntp master.

sections.title: Reading show ntp status and show ntp associations
sections.body:
Two commands prove NTP works, and exam exhibits use both.

**show ntp status** describes this device's own clock, and its first line carries what matters:

- `Clock is synchronized` or `Clock is unsynchronized`. Every client shows unsynchronized until it finishes synchronizing with at least one server, which can take several minutes after you configure it.
- `stratum 4`: this device's own stratum, its server's plus 1.
- `reference is 172.16.2.2`: the server it follows. A device running `ntp master` shows `127.127.1.1`, the address IOS uses to mean its own internal clock.

A device that has never synchronized shows `Clock is unsynchronized, stratum 16, no reference clock`.

**show ntp associations** lists one line per time source the device knows about:

- **address**: the server, as configured.
- **ref clock**: where that server gets its own time. `.LOCL.` means the server's internal clock, and `.INIT.` means the association is still initializing because the server has not answered.
- **st**: the server's stratum, not this device's. R1's line for R2 shows st 3, so R1 itself is 4.
- **when** and **poll**: seconds since the last reply, and the polling interval, which starts at 64 seconds and grows toward 1024 when the clock is stable.
- **reach**: an octal record of the last eight polls. 377 means all eight were answered; 0 means none were.
- The marks before the address: `*` is the **sys.peer**, the server the clock is actually following; `+` a candidate; `#` selected; `x` a falseticker it distrusts; `~` means the server was configured with a command.

On a server running `ntp master`, the association list shows its internal clock as `127.127.1.1` with ref clock `.LOCL.`, listed one stratum better than the stratum the router advertises.

A broken client usually reveals itself in these lines. A server stuck at `.INIT.` with reach 0 is not answering: check routing, an ACL that blocks UDP 123 or a mistyped address. A reachable server at stratum 16 has no good time to give.
sections.code:
R1# show ntp status
Clock is synchronized, stratum 4, reference is 172.16.2.2
nominal freq is 250.0000 Hz, actual freq is 250.0000 Hz, precision is 2**21
clock offset is 0.0986 msec, root delay is 2.46 msec

R1# show ntp associations
  address         ref clock       st   when   poll reach  delay  offset   disp
*~172.16.2.2      172.16.3.3       3     50     64   377  1.223   0.090  4.469
 * sys.peer, # selected, + candidate, - outlyer, x falseticker, ~ configured

R3# show ntp associations
  address         ref clock       st   when   poll reach  delay  offset   disp
*~127.127.1.1     .LOCL.           1     15     16   377  0.000   0.000  0.232
sections.tip: st in show ntp associations is the server's stratum. Your own stratum is in show ntp status.
sections.pitfall: Expecting a * the moment you type ntp server. Synchronization takes minutes; check reach and .INIT. before changing the configuration.

check.question: R1's association line for 10.1.1.1 reads `*~10.1.1.1  192.0.2.10  2  33  64  377`. What is R1's own stratum?
check.explanation: The st column shows the server's stratum, 2, and the * says R1 follows that server. A client adds 1, so R1 is stratum 3. Stratum 16 would mean unsynchronized, which the * rules out.

sections.title: Designing NTP: redundancy, fallback and loopbacks
sections.body:
One router as the only clock for a whole company is fragile. The official guide builds a sturdier design in four moves.

**Good, redundant sources.** Point a few core devices at two or more good servers, such as public stratum 1 servers or a GPS-based NTP appliance, with one `ntp server` line each. NTP compares them and follows the best. Every other router and switch then points at those core devices, never straight at the internet.

**A fallback clock.** If the core routers lose the internet, they lose their reference and stop being useful servers. Add `ntp master 7` (any stratum clearly worse than the real servers) as well. While the real servers answer, their lower stratum wins; when they disappear, the routers fall back to their own clocks, so the rest of the network still agrees on one time even if it drifts a little from true time.

**Loopback addresses.** A client points at one specific address of its server. If that address sits on a physical interface that fails, the client loses NTP even though the server is still reachable through other links. A loopback interface stays up as long as the router is up, so give the server one, advertise it in the routing protocol, point the clients at it, and add `ntp source loopback 0` on the server so its NTP packets always come from that address.

**Peers.** Two core routers can also be `ntp peer` of each other, so if one loses its servers it can follow the other.

Production networks also enable NTP authentication with `ntp authenticate`, `ntp authentication-key` and `ntp trusted-key`, so a device only accepts time from servers that know a shared key. A rogue time source is a real attack: shift a device's clock and you can make valid certificates look expired or blur when an intrusion happened.
sections.code:
! Core router R2: two outside servers and a fallback clock
R2(config)# ntp server 192.0.2.10
R2(config)# ntp server 192.0.2.11
R2(config)# ntp master 7
! R2 serves the site from a loopback that stays up
R2(config)# interface loopback 0
R2(config-if)# ip address 172.16.9.9 255.255.255.255
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# ntp source loopback 0

! Every other router and switch
SW1(config)# ntp server 172.16.9.9
sections.tip: Clients point at the server's loopback; the server sends NTP from that loopback with ntp source.
sections.pitfall: Giving the fallback ntp master a stratum as good as the real servers. The router may then trust its own drifting clock over them; use a clearly worse value such as 7 or 8.

check.question: Two core routers follow internet NTP servers. Which added command keeps them serving one consistent time to the site if the internet link fails?
check.explanation: ntp master with a stratum worse than the real servers is ignored while they answer and takes over when they do not. ntp master 1 would make the router's own clock compete with real stratum 1 servers, ntp source only picks the address NTP packets come from, and 127.127.1.1 is the internal clock, not a server to configure.

sections.title: Syslog messages: format and facilities
sections.body:
Unplug a cable on a Cisco router and the console immediately prints a line like the first one in the example. That is a **syslog message**, and every one of them has the same structure:

- **Timestamp**: when it happened, controlled by `service timestamps log datetime msec`. Only meaningful if the clock is right, and the asterisk again means it is not synchronized.
- **Facility**: `LINK` in the first message, the part of the system that generated it. Others you will see constantly: `LINEPROTO` (line protocol up or down), `SYS` (system events such as configuration changes), `OSPF`, `SEC_LOGIN`.
- **Severity**: a number from 0 (worst) to 7 (least important). `%LINK-3-UPDOWN` is severity 3.
- **Mnemonic**: `UPDOWN`, a short code for the specific message.
- **Description**: the human-readable text.

The pattern to remember is `%FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC: description`. Optionally a **sequence number** comes first (`service sequence-numbers`), which helps you notice missing messages.

The word facility has a second meaning in the syslog protocol itself. When a device sends messages to a syslog server, each one carries a protocol facility code, and network devices conventionally use `local0` through `local7`. Cisco IOS uses **local7** by default, and `logging facility local5` changes it so the server can sort different groups of devices into different files. For the exam, know both ideas: the facility in the message text names the IOS process, and the syslog facility (local0 to local7) labels the stream for the server.

Syslog to a server uses **UDP port 514**. It is unacknowledged and unencrypted, so treat it as best effort and keep a local copy of messages as well. Logging is also the first thing to check after any change: a `%SYS-5-CONFIG_I` message records who changed the configuration, from where and when.
sections.code:
*Mar  1 09:14:07.123: %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to down
*Mar  1 09:14:08.127: %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to down
*Mar  1 09:15:31.004: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from console by admin on vty0 (10.0.0.50)

Reading the first message:
  *Mar  1 09:14:07.123     timestamp (* means the clock is not synchronized)
  LINK                     facility
  3                        severity (errors)
  UPDOWN                   mnemonic
  Interface Gi0/1, ...     description
sections.pitfall: Assuming a higher severity number means a more serious message. It is the opposite: 0 is an emergency and 7 is debugging output.

check.question: In `%OSPF-5-ADJCHG: Process 1, Nbr 2.2.2.2 on Gi0/0 from FULL to DOWN`, what are the facility and the severity?
check.explanation: The format is %FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC: OSPF is the facility, 5 is the severity (notifications) and ADJCHG is the mnemonic. The process number in the text has nothing to do with severity.

sections.title: The eight severity levels
sections.body:
Every syslog message carries a severity from 0 to 7, and the CCNA expects you to know all eight, in order, by number and by name. **Lower numbers are more severe.**

The keywords you type in IOS logging commands are plural or slightly different from the everyday names (warnings, notifications, debugging), so learn both columns of the table.

A popular memory aid for the order 0 to 7: **Every Awesome Cisco Engineer Will Need Ice cream Daily** (Emergency, Alert, Critical, Error, Warning, Notification, Informational, Debugging).

How the levels group in practice:

- **0 and 1** are rare and serious: the system is unusable or someone must act now.
- **2, 3 and 4** describe problems affecting the device. An interface going down is level 3 (`%LINK-3-UPDOWN`).
- **5 and 6** are normal events worth recording. Line protocol changes, OSPF neighbor changes and configuration changes are level 5; many routine messages are level 6.
- **7** is debugging output, produced only while someone runs a debug command.

The rule that matters most for configuration: when you set a logging level, IOS sends messages at **that level and every more severe level**, meaning that number and all lower numbers. `logging trap 4` (or `logging trap warnings`) sends levels 0 through 4. `logging console 7` shows everything. There is no option to send only one level, or a range such as 2 to 5.

So choosing a level is a trade-off between noise and detail. Many teams send informational (6) to the syslog server, because storage is cheap and the extra detail helps later, while keeping the console quieter.
sections.code:
Level  IOS keyword      Name            Meaning
  0    emergencies      Emergency       System is unusable
  1    alerts           Alert           Immediate action needed
  2    critical         Critical        Critical condition
  3    errors           Error           Error condition (interface down)
  4    warnings         Warning         Warning condition
  5    notifications    Notification    Normal but significant (config change)
  6    informational    Informational   Informational message
  7    debugging        Debug           Output of debug commands

A configured level includes itself and every level above it in this table:
  logging trap warnings   sends 0, 1, 2, 3, 4   and drops 5, 6, 7
sections.tip: Every Awesome Cisco Engineer Will Need Ice cream Daily: 0 Emergency through 7 Debugging.
sections.pitfall: Configuring logging trap 6 and expecting only informational messages. A level includes everything more severe, so 6 sends levels 0 through 6.

check.question: Which command sends severity levels 0 through 4 to the syslog server?
check.explanation: Setting a level sends that level and everything more severe. Warnings is level 4, so logging trap warnings sends 0 through 4. IOS does not accept ranges, logging host names the server, and critical (2) would send only 0 through 2.

sections.title: Where log messages go
sections.body:
IOS can deliver each message to four destinations, and each destination has its own level:

- **Console** (`logging console [level]`): shown to whoever is on the console port. It is on by default at debugging, so console users see everything.
- **Monitor** (`logging monitor [level]`): shown to users connected by SSH or Telnet. The catch: each remote user must also type `terminal monitor` in their session. Without it nothing appears on a vty session, which surprises almost everyone the first time they run a debug over SSH.
- **Buffered** (`logging buffered [size] [level]`): stored in a RAM buffer on the device and read later with `show logging`. The buffer is lost on reload, and old messages roll off as new ones arrive.
- **Syslog server** (`logging host 10.0.0.50`, with `logging trap [level]`): sent over the network to a central server. The trap level defaults to informational. Odd name, but `logging trap` sets the level for syslog servers, not SNMP traps.

A central syslog server is the production standard: one searchable place for every device's history, kept even after a device reloads or fails. Many teams also set `logging source-interface loopback0` so each device's messages always arrive from the same address.

`show logging` confirms the whole setup at once: the level for each destination, the syslog server and its UDP port, and then the contents of the buffer.

Two quality-of-life commands round it out. `logging synchronous` under the console and vty lines stops log messages from breaking up the command you are typing. `no logging console` turns console messages off entirely, which some teams do on busy devices, relying on the buffer and the server instead.
sections.code:
R1(config)# logging console 7
R1(config)# logging buffered 16384 informational
R1(config)# logging host 10.0.0.50
R1(config)# logging trap warnings
R1(config)# end

R1# show logging
Syslog logging: enabled (0 messages dropped, 3 messages rate-limited, 0 flushes, 0 overruns)
    Console logging: level debugging, 45 messages logged
    Monitor logging: level debugging, 0 messages logged
    Buffer logging:  level informational, 12 messages logged
    Trap logging: level warnings, 7 message lines logged
        Logging to 10.0.0.50  (udp port 514, audit disabled, link up),
              7 message lines logged
Log Buffer (16384 bytes):
*Mar  1 09:14:07.123: %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to down
sections.pitfall: Running a debug over SSH and concluding nothing is happening. Type terminal monitor first, and remember that terminal no monitor turns it off again.

activity.title: Lab: send logs to a syslog server
activity.prompt: R1 must send its messages to the syslog server at 10.0.0.50, at informational level and more serious. Configure the host and the trap level, then run show logging and find the line that names the server and its UDP port.

check.question: An engineer connected by SSH runs `debug ip ospf adj` but sees no output, although logging monitor is at debugging. What is missing?
choices: The terminal monitor command in that SSH session
A logging host to receive the debug output
check.explanation: Messages reach a vty session only if logging monitor allows the level and the user has entered terminal monitor in that session. Console logging affects only the console port, and a syslog host is a separate destination.

sections.title: SNMP: managers, agents and the MIB
sections.body:
A network operations team watches 500 devices on one screen: interface graphs, CPU load, and a router icon that turns red the moment a link fails. Most of that comes from **SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol)**.

The pieces:

- **SNMP manager**: software on a **Network Management Station (NMS)** that polls devices, stores the data, draws graphs and raises alarms.
- **SNMP agent**: software on each managed device (router, switch, server, printer) that answers the manager and can send it notifications.
- **MIB (Management Information Base)**: the structured set of variables an agent exposes, such as interface status and counters, CPU load, hostname and uptime. A router exposes thousands of them.
- **OID (object identifier)**: the address of one MIB variable in a global tree of numbers. `1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0` is sysUpTime and `1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0` is sysName. Vendor-specific variables live under 1.3.6.1.4.1, with Cisco's branch at 1.3.6.1.4.1.9. People rarely type OIDs; the NMS shows friendly names.

The messages:

- **Get** (plus GetNext and, from SNMPv2, **GetBulk**): the manager reads variables and the agent answers with a **Response**.
- **Set**: the manager writes a variable to change the device, for example to shut down an interface. Powerful, so often not allowed at all.
- **Trap**: the agent reports an event without being asked, such as a link going down. It is fire and forget: no acknowledgment, so a lost trap stays lost.
- **Inform** (added in SNMPv2): like a trap, but the manager must acknowledge it, and the agent resends it if no acknowledgment arrives. More reliable, a little more overhead.

Ports: the agent listens on **UDP 161** for Get and Set requests, and the manager listens on **UDP 162** for traps and informs. Polling flows from manager to agent on 161; notifications flow from agent to manager on 162.

In practice teams combine both styles: **polling** every few minutes for graphs and trends, and **notifications** for immediate alerts.
sections.code:
NMS (SNMP manager)                        R1 (SNMP agent + MIB)
      |  Get ifOperStatus.2 (to UDP 161)  ------->  |
      |  <-------  Response: down(2)                 |
      |  Set ifAdminStatus.2 = up  -------------->  |
      |  <-------  Trap: linkDown (to UDP 162)       |  no acknowledgment
      |  <-------  Inform: linkDown (to UDP 162)     |  manager must acknowledge
      |  Response (acknowledgment)  ------------->  |
sections.pitfall: Mixing up the ports. Get and Set go to the agent on UDP 161; traps and informs go to the manager on UDP 162.

check.question: A router's interface fails and the NMS learns about it within a second, without polling. Which SNMP message did the router most likely send?
check.explanation: A trap is an unsolicited notification from the agent to the manager when an event happens. Get Response only answers a poll, Set is sent by the manager, and GetBulk is a manager request.

sections.title: SNMP versions and security
sections.body:
SNMP can read, and sometimes change, nearly everything on a device, so who may use it matters. The three versions differ mostly in security.

- **SNMPv1** uses **community strings**: shared passwords carried in **clear text** in every message. A **read-only (RO)** community allows Get; a **read-write (RW)** community allows Get and Set.
- **SNMPv2c** keeps the same community model (the c stands for community) and adds **GetBulk** and **Inform**. Still clear text. It is the most widely deployed version, which is exactly why exam questions ask about its weakness.
- **SNMPv3** replaces communities with **users and groups** and adds real security.

SNMPv3's security comes in three parts:

- **Message integrity and authentication**: messages are checked with a hash (such as SHA) keyed by the user's password, so tampering is detected and the password never crosses the network in clear text.
- **Privacy**: optional encryption of message contents (such as AES).
- **Security levels** that combine them: **noAuthNoPriv** (username only), **authNoPriv** (authentication, no encryption) and **authPriv** (authentication and encryption).

Whatever the version, defend in depth: restrict SNMP to the NMS addresses with an ACL, prefer read-only access, never keep the well-known defaults public and private, and use SNMPv3 with authPriv where you can.

A basic SNMPv2c configuration on IOS:

- `snmp-server community READONLY ro` creates a read-only community. Adding an ACL number at the end (`ro 10`) limits which hosts may use it.
- `snmp-server host 10.0.0.60 version 2c READONLY` sends notifications to the NMS using that community.
- `snmp-server enable traps` turns notifications on.
- `snmp-server location` and `snmp-server contact` fill in descriptive MIB variables the NMS displays.

The CCNA blueprint only asks you to explain SNMP, but configuring it once makes the ideas stick, and the console lab does exactly that.
sections.code:
R1(config)# access-list 10 permit host 10.0.0.60
R1(config)# snmp-server community READONLY ro 10
R1(config)# snmp-server location Building 2, rack 4
R1(config)# snmp-server contact noc@example.com
R1(config)# snmp-server host 10.0.0.60 version 2c READONLY
R1(config)# snmp-server enable traps
!
! The SNMPv3 equivalent: authenticated and encrypted
R1(config)# snmp-server group NMS-GROUP v3 priv
R1(config)# snmp-server user nms1 NMS-GROUP v3 auth sha AuthPass123 priv aes 128 PrivPass123
sections.pitfall: Treating SNMPv2c communities as secure passwords. They cross the network in clear text; anyone who captures one can read the device, or change it if the community is read-write.

activity.title: Lab: enable SNMP monitoring
activity.prompt: The NMS at 10.0.0.60 needs read-only access to R1 and should receive traps. Create a read-only community named READONLY, send traps to 10.0.0.60 using that community, and enable traps. Then think about what an attacker could do with a read-write community captured off the wire.

check.question: Which SNMP version provides authentication and encryption of SNMP messages?
choices: All versions, as long as a community string is set
check.explanation: Only SNMPv3 offers authentication (with integrity checking) and privacy (encryption), at the authPriv level. SNMPv1 and v2c rely on community strings sent in clear text.

sections.title: Putting it together: one outage, three protocols
sections.body:
Follow a single failure through all three services. At 02:14 the primary WAN link on branch router BR1 fails; BR1 still reaches headquarters over a backup link.

1. **Syslog.** BR1 generates `%LINK-3-UPDOWN` (severity 3, errors) for the serial interface, then `%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN` (severity 5, notifications). With `logging trap informational` both reach the syslog server at headquarters over UDP 514; with `logging trap errors` only the level 3 message would. Had the failed link been BR1's only path, both messages would have been lost on the way, which is why devices also keep a local copy with `logging buffered`.
2. **SNMP.** With `snmp-server enable traps` configured, BR1 sends a linkDown trap to the NMS on UDP 162 at once, and the router's icon turns red. If the trap were lost, the NMS would still notice at its next poll (to UDP 161) that the interface's status had changed. Polling catches what a lost trap misses.
3. **NTP.** The engineer on call now reads messages from BR1 and the hub router HQ1. BR1 follows the company NTP servers. HQ1 does not: its timestamp starts with an asterisk and reads March 1, the default date after its last reload. Nobody can tell from the logs whether HQ1 lost its OSPF neighbor at the same moment or hours earlier.

The fix is one command on HQ1, `ntp server` pointing at the company servers. Once it is synchronized, the two routers' messages line up to the millisecond and the story reads in order: the circuit failed, BR1's interface went down, and HQ1's OSPF neighbor timed out shortly after.

That is the division of labor to remember. Syslog records what each device saw, at a severity that decides where the message goes. SNMP raises the alarm and lets the NMS measure the network over time. NTP makes their timestamps agree, so the records from many devices tell one story.
sections.code:
Syslog server view (UDP 514), oldest first
Oct 21 02:14:07.311 BR1: %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface Serial0/0/0,
  changed state to down
Oct 21 02:14:08.315 BR1: %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on
  Interface Serial0/0/0, changed state to down
*Mar  1 00:41:55.120 HQ1: %OSPF-5-ADJCHG: Process 1, Nbr 10.9.9.1
  on Serial0/1/0 from FULL to DOWN, Neighbor Down: Dead timer expired

NMS view, traps received (UDP 162)
02:14:07  BR1  linkDown  Serial0/0/0
sections.tip: Syslog says what happened, SNMP says it right away, and NTP lets you put the two in order.
sections.pitfall: Relying on traps alone. A trap is sent once over UDP and is lost if the path to the NMS is down; polling and a local log buffer fill the gap.

check.question: In the exhibit, why can't the engineer tell whether HQ1's OSPF neighbor went down at the same moment as BR1's link?
choices: OSPF messages are severity 5, which the server stores without a timestamp
HQ1's clock was never synchronized, as the asterisk and the March 1 date show
HQ1 sends syslog over TCP, so its messages arrive late
Traps and syslog messages use different ports
check.explanation: An asterisk marks a clock that is not authoritative, and March 1 is a typical default date after a reload, so HQ1's timestamp cannot be compared with BR1's. Configuring NTP on HQ1 fixes it. Severity has nothing to do with timestamps, syslog uses UDP 514, and different ports do not affect correlation.

keyTerms.definition: Network Time Protocol: synchronizes device clocks over UDP 123.
Distance from a reference clock. Each NTP client adds 1 to its server's stratum; lower is better and 16 means unsynchronized.
Set with ntp server: the device synchronizes to a server, then can serve time to others.
Set with ntp master [stratum]: the device serves time from its own clock, default stratum 8.
The standard for device log messages; servers receive them on UDP 514.
In an IOS message, the process that generated it (LINK, SYS, OSPF). In the syslog protocol, a code such as local0 to local7; IOS defaults to local7.
0 emergencies, 1 alerts, 2 critical, 3 errors, 4 warnings, 5 notifications, 6 informational, 7 debugging. A configured level includes all more severe ones.
Sets the highest severity level number sent to syslog servers named with logging host. Default informational.
Software on a Network Management Station that polls agents and receives their notifications.
Software on a managed device that answers Get and Set on UDP 161 and sends traps and informs to UDP 162.
The MIB is the tree of variables an agent exposes; an OID such as 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0 identifies one variable.
The clear-text shared password of SNMPv1 and v2c, read-only (RO) or read-write (RW).
An authoritative time source such as GPS or an atomic clock. A server attached to one is stratum 1; IOS calls its own internal clock 127.127.1.1.
The server marked * in show ntp associations: the one the clock is actually following.
Agent-initiated SNMP notifications sent to the manager on UDP 162. A trap is never acknowledged; an inform is acknowledged and resent if needed.

summary: NTP (UDP 123) keeps clocks in sync so logs line up and certificates validate; ntp server makes a device a client (then a server), ntp master serves time from its own clock at default stratum 8, and ntp peer lets two devices back each other up.

Stratum counts hops from a reference clock: each client adds 1, lower wins and 16 means unsynchronized. In show ntp associations, * marks the sys.peer, st is the server's stratum and reach 377 means the last eight polls were answered.
Robust NTP uses two or more good servers on a few core devices, ntp master with a worse stratum as a fallback, and clients pointing at a loopback that the server sources NTP from.
Syslog messages read sequence number, timestamp, %FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC, description; servers receive them on UDP 514 with protocol facility local7 by default.

Severities run 0 to 7: emergencies, alerts, critical, errors, warnings, notifications, informational, debugging (Every Awesome Cisco Engineer Will Need Ice cream Daily). A configured level sends that level and everything more severe.
Logs go to the console, vty sessions (with terminal monitor), the RAM buffer (show logging) and syslog servers (logging host plus logging trap).
SNMP managers poll agents with Get and Set on UDP 161, agents send traps and informs to UDP 162; v1 and v2c use clear-text communities while v3 adds integrity, authentication and encryption.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a new junior engineer what happens when a WAN link fails at 2 a.m.: what message the router logs and at what severity, where that message goes, how the monitoring system finds out through SNMP, and why all the clocks have to agree.

questions.question: Which transport and port does NTP use?
questions.explanation: NTP uses UDP 123. UDP 514 is syslog and UDP 161 is SNMP polling.

questions.question: During an outage review, several routers' log timestamps start with an asterisk, such as `*Mar  1 00:42:17.311`. What does the asterisk mean, and what fixes it?
choices: The clock is not authoritative because it was never synchronized; configure NTP
The message was rate-limited; enlarge the logging buffer
The time is shown in UTC; configure clock timezone
The message came from a debug; turn off debugging
questions.explanation: An asterisk marks a clock that is not authoritative, typically one that was never synchronized (Mar 1 is a common default date after reload). Configuring NTP fixes the source of the problem; changing the time zone only changes how the time is displayed.

questions.question: Which command makes a router act purely as an NTP server based on its own internal clock?
questions.explanation: ntp master puts the device in server mode using its internal clock (default stratum 8). ntp server makes it a client of another server, and ntp source picks the interface address used for NTP packets.

questions.question: Type the global command that makes the router synchronize its clock to the NTP server at 10.0.0.1.
questions.explanation: ntp server puts the router in client/server mode: it synchronizes to 10.0.0.1 and can then serve time to others.

questions.question: R1 synchronizes to R2, R2 synchronizes to R3, and R3 runs `ntp master 2`. What is R1's stratum?
questions.explanation: Each client adds 1 to its server's stratum: R3 is 2, R2 becomes 3 and R1 becomes 4.

questions.question: Which stratum does a router use when it is configured with `ntp master` and no stratum value?
questions.explanation: The default for ntp master is stratum 8. Stratum 16 means unsynchronized, and stratum 1 is reserved in practice for servers attached to a real reference clock.

questions.question: Based on the exhibit, which statement is correct?
questions.code:
R2# show ntp associations
  address         ref clock       st   when   poll reach  delay  offset   disp
*~10.1.1.1        192.0.2.10       2     33     64   377  1.102   0.231  2.118
+~10.1.1.2        192.0.2.11       2     12     64   377  1.394   0.402  2.507
 ~10.9.9.9        .INIT.          16      -     64     0  0.000   0.000 15937.
 * sys.peer, # selected, + candidate, - outlyer, x falseticker, ~ configured
choices: R2 is synchronized to 10.1.1.1, and 10.9.9.9 has never answered
R2 is synchronized to 10.9.9.9 because it has the highest stratum
R2 is itself a stratum 2 server
10.1.1.2 is a falseticker and has been rejected
questions.explanation: The * marks the sys.peer, the server in use: 10.1.1.1. 10.9.9.9 shows .INIT., stratum 16 and reach 0, so it has never responded. R2 synchronizes to a stratum 2 server, which makes R2 stratum 3. The + on 10.1.1.2 means candidate, not falseticker (x).

questions.question: What does the exhibit tell you about R1?
questions.code:
R1# show ntp status
Clock is unsynchronized, stratum 16, no reference clock
choices: R1 is a stratum 16 server, the most accurate level
R1 is running ntp master with the default stratum
R1 has not synchronized with any NTP server yet
R1 is synchronized but has no hardware clock
questions.explanation: Stratum 16 with no reference clock means unsynchronized. Either no server is configured, none is reachable, or synchronization has not finished yet. An ntp master device would show synchronized, stratum 8 by default.

questions.question: Which two statements about NTP stratum are true? (Choose two.)
choices: A client's stratum is its server's stratum plus 1
Lower stratum values are considered more accurate
Stratum 16 is the most accurate level
Stratum counts the NTP packets exchanged so far
questions.explanation: Stratum is the distance from the reference clock: each hop adds 1 and lower is better. Stratum 16 means unsynchronized, and ntp master defaults to stratum 8.

questions.question: R1 has `ntp server 10.1.1.1`, `ntp server 10.1.1.2` and `ntp master 10`. Both servers are reachable and run at stratum 2. What does R1 use as its time source?
choices: Its internal clock, because ntp master overrides ntp server
One of the NTP servers, because their stratum is better than its own clock's 10
Both servers alternately, switching every poll interval
Nothing; the commands conflict and NTP stops
questions.explanation: NTP prefers the lowest stratum available. The servers at stratum 2 beat the internal clock at 10, so R1 follows a server and only falls back to its own clock if both become unreachable. That is exactly why the fallback uses a high stratum.

questions.question: In `%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface Gi0/1, changed state to up`, what is UPDOWN?
questions.explanation: The pattern is %FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC: LINEPROTO is the facility, 5 the severity and UPDOWN the mnemonic.

questions.question: Which UDP port does a syslog server listen on for messages from network devices?
questions.explanation: Syslog uses UDP 514. 162 receives SNMP traps, 123 is NTP and 69 is TFTP.

questions.question: A syslog server sorts incoming messages into files by syslog facility. Which facility does Cisco IOS use by default when it sends messages to a server?
questions.explanation: IOS tags messages sent to syslog servers with facility local7 unless you change it with logging facility. Network devices conventionally use local0 to local7, and kern and user are used by operating systems.

questions.question: Put the syslog severity levels in order from most severe (level 0) to least severe (level 7).
questions.explanation: Every Awesome Cisco Engineer Will Need Ice cream Daily: 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notification, 6 Informational, 7 Debugging.

questions.question: Match each IOS logging keyword to its severity level.
questions.explanation: The full list is emergencies 0, alerts 1, critical 2, errors 3, warnings 4, notifications 5, informational 6, debugging 7. Lower numbers are more severe.

questions.question: `%LINK-3-UPDOWN` reports an interface going down. Which IOS logging keyword names severity level 3?
questions.explanation: Level 3 is errors (error condition). Level 2 is critical and level 4 is warnings.

questions.question: Which messages does `logging trap notifications` send to the syslog server?
questions.explanation: Notifications is level 5, and a configured level includes itself and all more severe (lower-numbered) levels, so 0 through 5 are sent.

questions.question: Syslog must capture configuration changes (`%SYS-5-CONFIG_I`) but nothing less severe. Which trap level should you configure?
questions.explanation: Configuration changes are level 5. Notifications (5) captures levels 0 through 5 and excludes 6 and 7. Warnings or errors would miss the level 5 messages, and informational would also include level 6.

questions.question: Type the global command that sends log messages to a syslog server at 10.0.0.50.
questions.explanation: logging host names a syslog server. The level sent to it is set separately with logging trap, which defaults to informational.

questions.question: Type the global command that limits the messages sent to the syslog server to warnings and more severe.
questions.explanation: logging trap sets the level for syslog servers. Warnings is level 4, so levels 0 through 4 are sent.

questions.question: Which command displays the messages stored with logging buffered?
questions.explanation: show logging lists the logging settings for every destination and then the contents of the RAM log buffer. show buffers is about packet memory buffers, not log messages.

questions.question: An engineer logged in over SSH wants log messages to appear in the session as they happen. Which command does the engineer type in that session?
questions.explanation: terminal monitor is an EXEC command that asks IOS to copy log messages to this vty session (subject to the logging monitor level). logging monitor is the global setting for the level; on its own it does not turn on messages for a session.

questions.question: An interface flaps, producing `%LINK-3-UPDOWN` and `%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN`. Of the console, the buffer and the syslog server, where is the LINEPROTO message recorded?
questions.code:
R1# show logging
Syslog logging: enabled (0 messages dropped, 0 messages rate-limited, 0 flushes, 0 overruns)
    Console logging: level debugging, 210 messages logged
    Monitor logging: level debugging, 0 messages logged
    Buffer logging:  level warnings, 18 messages logged
    Trap logging: level errors, 9 message lines logged
        Logging to 10.0.0.50  (udp port 514, audit disabled, link up),
              9 message lines logged
choices: The console, the buffer and the server
questions.explanation: LINEPROTO is level 5. The console logs up to debugging (7), so it shows it. The buffer keeps only 0 to 4 (warnings) and the server gets only 0 to 3 (errors), so neither records it. The level 3 LINK message, by contrast, reaches all three.

questions.question: Which SNMP component runs on the managed router or switch?
questions.explanation: The agent runs on each managed device and exposes its MIB. The manager runs on the Network Management Station and polls agents.

questions.question: Match each SNMP message to what it does.

pairs.right: The manager reads a variable from the agent
The manager changes a variable on the agent
The agent reports an event with no acknowledgment
The agent reports an event and expects an acknowledgment
The manager reads many variables in one request

questions.explanation: Get, GetBulk and Set come from the manager; Trap and Inform come from the agent. Inform and GetBulk were added in SNMPv2.

questions.question: Which statement about SNMP ports is correct?
choices: Agents receive Get and Set on UDP 162; managers receive traps on UDP 161
Traps use UDP 514, the same port as syslog
Agents receive Get and Set on UDP 161; managers receive traps and informs on UDP 162
questions.explanation: Polling goes to the agent on UDP 161, and notifications go to the manager on UDP 162. SNMP runs over UDP, and 514 belongs to syslog.

questions.question: What is an OID in SNMP?
choices: The numeric identifier of one MIB variable in a global tree
The password an NMS uses to read a device
The IP address of the SNMP manager
The name of a group of SNMPv3 users
questions.explanation: Each MIB variable has an object identifier such as 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0 (sysName). Passwords are community strings or SNMPv3 user credentials.

questions.question: An NMS must receive failure notifications reliably, even across a lossy WAN link. What should the routers send?
choices: GetBulk responses, because they carry more data
Informs, because the manager acknowledges them and the agent resends if needed
Set requests, because they always get a response
questions.explanation: Informs add application-layer reliability: the manager acknowledges each one and the agent retries if it hears nothing. Traps are fire and forget over UDP, like every SNMP message.

questions.question: What is the main security weakness of SNMPv2c?
choices: Community strings are sent in clear text
It requires TCP, which attackers can hijack
questions.explanation: v1 and v2c authenticate with community strings carried in clear text, so anyone who captures a packet learns the community. SNMPv2c does send traps (and informs), runs over UDP and supports read-only communities.

questions.question: Which three features does SNMPv3 add compared with SNMPv2c? (Choose three.)
questions.explanation: SNMPv3 replaces communities with users and adds integrity, authentication and optional privacy (encryption). Communities and UDP existed before, and Inform arrived with SNMPv2.

questions.question: Type the global command that creates a read-only SNMP community named READONLY.
questions.explanation: snmp-server community name ro creates a read-only community (rw would allow Set). You can add an ACL number at the end to limit which hosts may use it.

questions.question: An NMS graphs R1's interfaces fine, but every attempt to shut down an interface through SNMP fails. Based on the exhibit, why?
questions.code:
R1# show running-config | include snmp-server
snmp-server community MONITOR RO
snmp-server location HQ rack 4
snmp-server host 10.0.0.60 version 2c MONITOR
choices: The NMS must use traps to change settings
SNMPv2c does not support the Set message
The community is read-only, so Set requests are refused
questions.explanation: A read-only community permits Get but not Set. Changing a device through SNMP needs a read-write community or an SNMPv3 user with write access. Set exists in every SNMP version.

questions.question: Which SNMPv3 security level authenticates messages and also encrypts them?
questions.explanation: authPriv provides both authentication and privacy (encryption). authNoPriv authenticates without encrypting, noAuthNoPriv uses only a username, and privNoAuth does not exist.

questions.question: Why does accurate, synchronized time matter on network devices?
questions.answer: So log timestamps from different devices line up during troubleshooting and investigations, and so time-sensitive security works: certificates have validity dates, and authentication and time-based features depend on the clock.
questions.explanation: NTP over UDP 123 provides this automatically; an asterisk on a timestamp warns you the clock was never synchronized.

questions.question: Type the global command that makes R3 serve time from its own internal clock at stratum 3.
questions.explanation: ntp master puts the device in server mode using its internal clock. The number sets the stratum it advertises; without one it uses 8.

questions.question: R2 serves NTP to the site from its Loopback0 address. Type the global command that makes R2 send its NTP packets from that loopback.
questions.explanation: ntp source sets the interface whose address NTP packets come from. Pairing it with clients that point at the loopback keeps NTP working when any single physical interface fails.

questions.question: R2 shows the exhibit. What does it tell you about 10.1.1.2?
questions.code:
R2# show ntp associations
  address         ref clock       st   when   poll reach  delay  offset   disp
*~10.1.1.1        192.0.2.10       2     33     64   377  1.102   0.231  2.118
+~10.1.1.2        192.0.2.11       2     41     64    17  1.394   0.402  3.507
 * sys.peer, # selected, + candidate, - outlyer, x falseticker, ~ configured
choices: It is the server R2 is following right now
It has answered only its last four polls, typical of a server that was just configured or just came back
It is a falseticker that R2 refuses to use
It is 17 milliseconds away from R2
questions.explanation: Reach is an 8-bit record of the last eight polls, shown in octal. 377 is 11111111 in binary, so 10.1.1.1 answered all of its last eight polls; 17 is 00001111, so 10.1.1.2 answered only the last four. A newly configured or recovered server climbs 1, 3, 7, 17, 37, 77, 177, 377. The * marks 10.1.1.1 as the sys.peer, the + makes 10.1.1.2 a candidate rather than a falseticker (x), and delay has its own column.

questions.question: Which NTP command on R3 best explains the exhibit?
questions.code:
R3# show ntp status
Clock is synchronized, stratum 8, reference is 127.127.1.1
questions.explanation: 127.127.1.1 is how IOS names its own internal clock, so R3 serves time from itself: server mode. Stratum 8 is the default for ntp master with no value. 127.127.1.1 is not a server you configure, and ntp source only picks the address NTP packets are sent from.

questions.question: Core routers R1 and R2 use `ntp server` to two internet stratum 1 servers and also run `ntp master 7`. The internet link fails for an hour. What happens to time in the enterprise?
choices: Every client becomes unsynchronized until the link returns
R1 and R2 fall back to their own clocks at stratum 7, so clients stay synchronized to one consistent time
R1 and R2 announce stratum 1 because they are now the only reference
NTP stops on R1 and R2 because ntp master and ntp server conflict
questions.explanation: With the servers unreachable, the internal clock at stratum 7 is the best source left, so R1 and R2 keep serving time and their clients stay in step, perhaps drifting slightly from true time. When the internet servers return, their lower stratum wins again. The two commands are meant to work together.

questions.question: Clients use `ntp server 10.1.4.4`, the address of R4's G0/0. G0/0 fails, but routing converges and R4 is still reachable through G0/1. What happens, and what is the better design?
choices: Nothing changes, because NTP follows the routing table to R4
The clients switch to R4's G0/1 address automatically
The clients lose that server because 10.1.4.4 is down; point them at a loopback on R4 and add ntp source loopback 0 on R4
The clients become stratum 1, because R4 is no longer in the path
questions.explanation: Clients send to one specific address, and an address on a down interface cannot answer even if the router is reachable another way. A loopback stays up as long as the router does, so clients that point at it, plus ntp source on the server, survive any single interface failure.

questions.question: With timestamps and sequence numbers turned on, put the fields of an IOS log message in the order they appear.
questions.explanation: For example `000045: *Mar  1 09:14:07.123: %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface Gi0/1, changed state to down`: sequence number, timestamp, then %FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC and the readable description. Sequence numbers are off by default and turned on with service sequence-numbers.

questions.question: Match each log destination to how it is configured.

pairs.right: logging monitor, plus terminal monitor in the session
logging buffered, read with show logging
logging host, with the level set by logging trap

questions.explanation: Each destination has its own level. Remote sessions need both the global logging monitor level and terminal monitor in that session, and the buffer is lost at reload, which is why production networks also send to a server.

questions.question: Which OID prefix leads to Cisco's vendor-specific MIB variables?
questions.explanation: 1.3.6.1.4.1 is the private enterprises branch and 9 is Cisco's number, so Cisco-specific variables live under 1.3.6.1.4.1.9. 1.3.6.1.2.1 is the standard MIB-2 tree, where .1 is the system group (sysName, sysUpTime) and .2 the interfaces group, and 1.3.6.1.6.3.15 belongs to the SNMPv3 security model.

questions.question: Which two SNMP messages does an agent send to the manager without being asked first? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: Traps and informs are notifications the agent sends when something happens, to the manager on UDP 162. Get, GetBulk and Set are requests the manager sends to the agent on UDP 161.

questions.question: R1's only WAN link, its path to the NMS, failed and later recovered. Based on the exhibit, what most likely happened to the linkDown trap?
questions.code:
R1# show logging | include UPDOWN
Oct 21 02:14:07.311: %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface Serial0/0/0, changed state to down
Oct 21 02:31:44.902: %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface Serial0/0/0, changed state to up

NMS event log for R1
02:18:00  poll failed, no response (UDP 161)
02:32:00  poll succeeded, Serial0/0/0 up
choices: R1 never sends traps for severity 3 events
R1 sent the trap, but it was lost on the failed path, and traps are never acknowledged or resent
The NMS listens for traps on UDP 161, the port it polls
R1 needs SNMPv3 before it can send traps
questions.explanation: The local buffer proves the interface went down at 02:14:07, yet the NMS only learned of trouble at 02:18 when a poll went unanswered. Traps are fire and forget over UDP: if the path is down, the trap is lost and nothing resends it. Informs would be retried, and polling caught the failure anyway. Severity levels belong to syslog, managers receive traps on UDP 162, and every SNMP version supports traps.
